paragraphs: SENAWANG, Malaysia—An hour outside of the Malaysian capital, Bangladeshi workers this past week were driving dump trucks and excavators at a site stretching across 117 football fields.

It was a world away from the Silicon Valley boardroom where, hours later, Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang would be ousted. Yet this site in Southeast Asia and others like it are at the heart of the Huang affair.

Here, a Chinese company plans to use Nvidia’s advanced artificial-intelligence chips. Thanks to Chinese customers, data-center industry leaders say Malaysia could become the second-largest data center hub in the world, after Virginia, packed with top-of-the-line Nvidia chips China’s leading AI companies can use to challenge American dominance.

Huang built a multibillion-dollar business to feed the ravenous appetite of Chinese customers for American chips, cultivating a network of Asian partners who could serve the Chinese far from Washington. He made a friend of President Trump and lobbied Washington hard to keep the backdoor to China open.
Kang Wei’s investment firm owned a 27 percent stake in a data center developer, while his wife gained access to Nvidia’s chip supply chain.

The husband of Alice Huang — a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and having an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — has reportedly pursued a massive data center project backed by the Chinese government.

Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband, had planned more than $9 billion in data center investments from 2021 through 2024, the Wall Street Journal reported Monday after examining Chinese corporate disclosures and official government statements.
Long before the alleged affair, Kang and the Nvidia founder had become acquainted through the video game business. Kang reportedly set up an introduction to his wife himself.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Kang appeared to have quietly acquiesced to the relationship between his wife and Jensen Huang, according to acquaintances of the couple.
Kang's foray into the data center project began in late 2021, ahead of Washington's move to curb shipments of cutting-edge AI semiconductors to China.

The venture revolved around Century Longteng, a data center developer headquartered in Shanghai. At the time, the Chinese gaming company Century Huatong was its largest shareholder with a 63 percent stake. A Kang-linked investment firm owned 27 percent, and an agency under the Shanghai city government held the other 10 percent.
Huawei, the Chinese telecom equipment maker targeted by U.S. sanctions, agreed with Century Longteng in early 2022 to jointly develop cloud data centers and computing facilities.

Century Longteng announced a $4.5 billion investment in data center construction in Wuhu, a city in Anhui Province, in the summer of 2022. The project received state backing for electricity and infrastructure as part of Beijing's push to expand computing capacity. By April this year, at least one data center building had been officially registered as complete.

Kang also attended a groundbreaking ceremony for a $5 billion data center project in Liangshan, Sichuan Province, in July 2024. He was also reportedly involved in similar ventures in Shenzhen, a major technology hub in southern China.
As her husband expanded his data center business across China, Alice Huang gained access to Nvidia's chip supply chain through the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.
Singaporean authorities reportedly identified Alice Huang as Megaspeed’s CEO and one of its key controllers at the time.

The company secured cloud partner status with Nvidia in November 2023 after presenting Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba as a major customer. Some of the Nvidia chips the company obtained reportedly made their way into China.

The Wall Street Journal cautioned that there was no confirmation that Alice Huang had acquired Nvidia chips on orders from Chinese authorities or that the semiconductors had ended up in Kang's data center projects.

At least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia processors reached China through Alice Huang, who reportedly leveraged her personal ties to Jensen Huang, U.S. technology outlet The Information previously reported.
Authorities in the United States and Singapore are investigating Megaspeed over suspected violations of chip export controls.

The company, on its part, has maintained that its operations were lawful and that Alice Huang no longer held any position at the company. The Wall Street Journal said it had sought comment from both Kang and Alice Huang but received no response.
BY HYEON YE-SEUL [lee.soojung1@joongang.co.kr]

paragraphs: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday blamed Friday’s air-travel outage that caused havoc at airports nationwide on work being done to replace copper wires with fiber ones at a single remote facility.
He pointed the finger at the work of contractor L3Harris, which either installed a faulty router or was “not doing great work for us,” Duffy told reporters on Saturday.
“So what we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence,” Duffy said. “Frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

L3Harris Technologies, which has worked with the Federal Aviation Administration for decades, said that it is supporting the FAA’s investigation. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” it said.

https://www.wsj.com/finance/corporate-ca.title: Corporate-Card Startup Ramp Raising Funds at $70 Billion Valuation
https://www.wsj.com/finance/corporate-ca.author: Kate Clark
paragraphs: Fintech company is reportedly seeking at least $1 billion after doubling annualized revenue to $2 billion.

Ramp, the fast-growing corporate-card and financial-management technology company, is in preliminary discussions to raise at least $1 billion at a valuation exceeding $70 billion, potentially marking its third financing round in a year.

The proposed investment would further increase Ramp’s valuation, which has more than doubled over the past 12 months as businesses increasingly adopt its financial software and artificial intelligence tools.

Existing investors Coatue Management and Thrive Capital, founded by Josh Kushner, are reportedly discussing leading the financing, according to The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the negotiations.
Founded in 2019 and led by CEO Eric Glyman, Ramp has rapidly emerged as one of the most valuable privately held financial technology companies.
In October, the company announced that its annualized revenue had surpassed $2 billion, roughly double what it was a year earlier.
Ramp also completed a $1.85 billion financing round last month at a $60 billion valuation. A new round exceeding $70 billion would represent at least a 16.7% increase in just weeks.
The company’s corporate-card business still generates most of its revenue, but its broader financial-management platform is becoming an increasingly important growth driver.
Ramp expects revenue from other services, including bill payments and banking, to surpass its corporate-card revenue within the next year.
AI Spending Creates New Growth Opportunities
Artificial intelligence has become a key part of Ramp’s expansion strategy.
The company is benefiting from rising corporate spending on AI services while developing tools that help businesses monitor and control those expenses.
Its Router product, for example, helps companies manage AI-related expenditures, addressing a growing challenge as enterprises deploy multiple AI models, applications and subscription services.

The expansion reflects Ramp’s strategy of evolving beyond corporate credit cards into a comprehensive financial-management platform that combines payments, expense controls, automation and AI-powered software.
Acquisition Strategy and Potential IPO
Ramp is expected to use part of the proceeds from its proposed financing to pursue mergers and acquisitions, potentially expanding its product offerings and market reach.
The company could pursue an initial public offering as early as 2027, although no formal timetable has been established.
Investors are closely monitoring the market for technology IPOs, including Anthropic’s anticipated public offering, as a potential indicator of investor demand for high-growth technology companies.
Ramp’s existing investor base includes Thrive Capital, Coatue Management, D1 Capital Partners, Founders Fund and Redpoint Ventures.
At a valuation exceeding $70 billion, Ramp would further strengthen its position among the world’s most valuable privately held technology companies.
The proposed transaction remains in preliminary discussions, and its final size, valuation and participating investors could change.

paragraphs: Revenue increased 10% to RMB271.519 billion ($40.498 billion), according to the company’s earnings release. Non-GAAP net income rose 92% to RMB19.909 billion, while adjusted diluted earnings per American depositary share increased 86% to RMB8.10 ($1.21). Each ADS represents eight ordinary shares.

The stock traded at $83.00, down $1.37, or 1.62%, in a premarket quotation timestamped 6:54 a.m. EST on November 19, 2026. Its November 18 closing price was $84.37 at 4 p.m. EST. Research and market data were checked at 7:04 a.m. EST; premarket prices can move sharply in thinner trading.

Reuters reported that revenue exceeded an LSEG consensus of RMB269.81 billion, but adjusted earnings per ADS missed expectations of RMB11.16. The mixed result helps explain why faster cloud growth did not immediately lift the shares.
Reported net income attributable to ordinary shareholders rose 207% to RMB64.535 billion, benefiting from investment gains excluded from adjusted earnings.

AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue increased 53% to RMB60.973 billion. External-customer recurring revenue grew 67%, excluding compute-equipment solutions. The segment’s adjusted earnings before interest, tax and amortisation increased 121% to RMB8.838 billion, with a 14.5% margin.

That improvement did not cover the losses in a separate AI business. AI Labs and Applications recorded an adjusted EBITA loss of RMB10.503 billion, against RMB3.435 billion a year earlier. Revenue in that unit increased 51% to RMB4.435 billion, but investment in AI capabilities and higher Qwen application inference costs weighed on profitability.

Capital expenditure reached RMB50.477 billion. Operating cash flow increased 55% to RMB15.690 billion, yet company-defined free cash flow deteriorated to an outflow of RMB34.472 billion from RMB21.840 billion. Over six months, free-cash outflow totalled RMB79.142 billion.

Alibaba retained RMB487.929 billion in cash and other liquid investments at September 30. Its balance-sheet bank borrowings and listed categories of notes and exchangeable bonds totalled a calculated RMB267.209 billion. The broad liquidity measure includes treasury investments; it is larger than cash alone.

Financing also carries a shareholder cost. The company raised net proceeds of HK$80 billion through new shares during the half year. Quarterly weighted-average diluted ordinary shares used for non-GAAP earnings increased to 19,777 million from 19,168 million, showing dilution alongside the investment programme.

The commerce picture remained uneven. China e-commerce revenue declined 5%, although customer-management revenue would have risen 1% excluding a subsidy-related accounting effect. International e-commerce revenue fell 8%, partly because EU customs reforms affected AliExpress. Alibaba E-commerce Group’s adjusted EBITA nevertheless increased 243%, helped by improved quick-commerce operations.

Broker targets remain much higher than the share price. Dated records show Goldman Sachs at Buy/$177 on November 19, Bernstein at a provider-normalised Buy/$165 on November 18, Bank of America at Buy/$178 on November 11, and Mizuho at a provider-normalised Buy/$200 on November 3.

Earlier assessments include J.P. Morgan’s Overweight/$200 on October 12, Jefferies’ Buy/$192 on October 8 and UBS’s Buy/$206 on September 22. Most predate these results; Goldman’s same-day entry does not establish whether its assessment followed the release.

Alibaba’s stronger cloud economics are offset by AI development losses and negative free cash flow. Its published trailing earnings multiple of 19.26 compares with 18.99 at fiscal 2026 year-end and JD.com’s (Nasdaq:JD) 15.23. Investment gains, different business models and database timing limit those comparisons.

Over the next 12 months, monitor external cloud growth, AI spending relative to cash generation, and commerce profitability. Slower cloud demand, persistent application losses or further dilutive financing without better cash returns would weaken the recovery case.

https://www.wsj.com/business/earnings/te.title: Temu Owner Reports Flat Profit, Revenue as Challenges Continue
https://www.wsj.com/business/earnings/te.author: Wall Street Journal
paragraphs: Published on 11/19/2026 at 07:43 am EST
The Chinese owner of bargain-shopping app Temu posted flat earnings as it continued to deal with subdued consumer sentiment at home and regulatory pressures abroad.

Still, the results ended a string of profit declines for PDD Holdings, whose profitability has been under pressure in recent quarters it strengthens its e-commerce ecosystem. The company has also faced challenges in overseas markets amid tightened regulatory requirements and geopolitical tensions.

The company behind Temu and Chinese platform Pinduoduo on Thursday said net profit edged 0.7% higher from a year earlier to 29.54 billion yuan, equivalent to $4.43 billion. Revenue was little changed at 108.34 billion yuan.
Analysts had expected net profit of 24.81 billion yuan on revenue of 115.67 billion yuan, according to a FactSet consensus.
"We remain in a strategic investment phase, focused on strengthening supply-chain capabilities and supporting our merchants," said Jun Liu, vice president of finance.

PDD's American depositary receipts rose nearly 9% premarket, pointing to brightening investor sentiment. Appetite for the Nasdaq-listed company has waned as sentiment on tech companies weakened, leaving PDD's stock down by about one third this year.

Citi analysts pointed to Temu's shrinking user base, with Europe leading the decline as PDD faces tighter regulations in the bloc. Temu's global monthly active users fell 17.8% on iOS and 11.2% on Android in September, Citi said, citing third-party estimates.

Adding to its headwinds, the European Commission earlier this week said measures Temu put in place to tackle illegal products sold on its platform were insufficient, including what it called a "weak" content moderation system and ineffective sanctions. A PDD spokesperson said the company disagrees with the commission's view and will respond to the findings.

Meanwhile, back home, subdued consumer sentiment is weighing on Pinduoduo's performance. Total retail sales of consumer goods grew just 1.1% during the first nine months of 2026, official data showed. Sales for this year's Singles' Day--China's biggest online-shopping event of the year--rose 4.8% from last year, according to data provider Syntun.

paragraphs: WASHINGTON—Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings that U.S. artificial-intelligence chips were being smuggled to China before the recent Nvidia scandal became public, a top Republican senator said, the latest sign that lawmakers are blaming the Commerce Department for the potential security crisis.

In an interview, Sen. Tom Cotton (R., Ark.), a longtime China hawk who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, stopped short of saying Lutnick should resign or be fired as Commerce secretary, but he declined to support him.

paragraphs: Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.
Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.

Founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.

Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the company announced it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.

Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The company has outlined ambitious growth plans, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.

Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit company Blue Apron, restaurant delivery platform Grubhub, media company Tastemade, and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.

Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create, its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop new food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.
Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.

Despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.

o The deal talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, the report said

paragraphs: SINGAPORE—Jensen Huang’s romantic partner was the public face of a business suspected of funneling advanced computing power to China. But playing a key role behind the scenes, according to people familiar with the matter, was a man now out on bail in Singapore, living in a luxury villa down the street from the Chinese embassy.

His name is Li Ming. The 52-year-old Chinese national was a central operator of a web of companies smuggling restricted Nvidia artificial-intelligence chips to China, the people said. This web included Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Huang’s paramour, Alice Huang, was a managing director. Li was deeply involved in Megaspeed’s activities and took part in major decisions, the people said, as well as playing a role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.

paragraphs: Two years before she pulled off the largest public offering of all time, Daniela Amodei gathered everyone at Anthropic in a 16-acre garden on a sweltering fall day near the Santa Cruz mountains.

The AI company now with a market value of roughly $1.18 trillion was at the time still a young startup that Amodei and her big brother, Dario, had co-founded with five friends. It was undergoing a hiring spree and Daniela was worried. So they carted 10-foot-tall bookshelves onto the grass to make reading nooks, played games and made friendship bracelets. As the company’s president, and keeper of its culture, the younger Amodei wanted to deliver a message.
“Keep Anthropic weird,” Daniela told them.

Anthropic embraces being atypical because it believes the artificial intelligence future will be anything but normal. Many co-founders meet in college, or at a first job. This pair met when he was 4 and she was born.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei have defended the artificial intelligence (AI) company's massive infrastructure commitments and reiterated their focus on responsible AI development, saying its record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) will not change its long-term mission.

Speaking to CNBC International ahead of Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, the siblings addressed the company's $900 billion AI commitments, its approach to balancing growth with safety, partnerships with major technology companies and its relationship with the US government.
Daniela Amodei described the IPO as a significant milestone but said the company would remain focused on its original objectives.

Addressing questions around Anthropic's substantial AI infrastructure spending, Dario Amodei defended commitments of around $900 billion, arguing that they should be viewed in the context of the company's cash reserves and growing revenue.
Amodei added that Anthropic tries to "err on the low side" when forecasting its computing requirements.
He also acknowledged the challenge of balancing the pace of AI development with safety considerations, describing it as one of the company's central tensions.

"What we've done with pacing is essentially said, look, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour. Spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus we spend building the model in the right way," he said.
On the expectations surrounding Anthropic's public market debut, Amodei said the company was keeping its focus on execution rather than the spotlight.
"We've been calm about it," he said, adding that Anthropic's approach was to "always want to under promise and over deliver".
Daniela Amodei said safety remained central to Anthropic's approach, arguing that the potential benefits of AI must be balanced against the risks associated with the technology.

"The promise is incredible, and the risks are real. And we were really founded on this idea that it is our job to mitigate those risks," she said, adding that the company remained deeply committed to safety.
She also highlighted Anthropic's public benefit structure, saying the company wanted its economic value and broader mission to be embedded in its organisational framework.
On data centre expansion, Daniela said Anthropic would need to listen to local communities and take their concerns into account.

Dario Amodei described Anthropic's relationship with Nvidia as a "long and productive partnership". He also expressed satisfaction with its work with SpaceX amid speculation about whether the company could scale back its use of the Elon Musk-led company's computing capacity.
"We're finding that compute to be high quality. We're enjoying working with SpaceX," he said.
On Anthropic's differences with the US Department of Defense, Daniela Amodei said there were no significant updates but expected the company's relationship with the government to continue.
She said Anthropic had worked closely with the US national security establishment since its founding and remained committed to ensuring that its Claude AI models could help protect the country.
Dario Amodei also said Anthropic hoped to secure an investment-grade credit rating in the future, adding that debt was an instrument the company would like to use at some point.
Anthropic is set for its Nasdaq debut on Thursday after raising more than $81 billion in a record-breaking IPO, surpassing SpaceX's offering in June.
The Claude creator sold 980 million shares at $83 apiece on Wednesday, taking its fully diluted market capitalisation to around $1.5 trillion.

The five-year-old company has seen rapid growth on the back of its Claude AI models and products. According to its prospectus, Anthropic generated $33.24 billion in revenue in the nine months ended September 30, up 1,200% from the same period last year.
Speaking at Nasdaq, Amodei highlighted AI's potential to advance medicine and help cure diseases, while reiterating the importance of responsible development.
"Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing," he said.
"If we can show it's possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same," he added.

paragraphs: French and U.S. authorities suspect Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe, an incident that reportedly spoiled food and caused equipment failures, resulting in tens of millions of dollars in damage. The attack affected about 700 supermarkets, raising concerns about the exposure of connected refrigeration systems and the potential for cyber operations to disrupt essential commercial infrastructure.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot accused Tehran of orchestrating the attack, warning that Iran would face retribution. Speaking Monday at a Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Paris, Barrot described the incident as the first large-scale cyberattack conducted for sabotage on French national territory, calling it a major threat to the country’s interests and the security of its population.

“Following its investigation, France is able to attribute these destructive actions to Iran, carried out by the SHAHID KAVEH cyber offensive unit, affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” France’s Foreign Ministry wrote in a Monday statement attributing cyberattacks targeting France to Iran. “This actor poses a persistent threat to our critical infrastructure.”

It added that these destructive cyberattacks are unjustifiable, inexcusable, and violate international law. “They also contravene the principles of the United Nations’ normative framework for responsible state behavior in cyberspace, to which the Islamic Republic of Iran has subscribed.”

The agency highlighted that the Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024. In March 2026, the European Union adopted sanctions against the Iranian entity Emmenet Pasargad, which had contributed to conducting these cyberattacks.”

During the night of October 11-12, a cyberattack campaign targeted supermarket refrigeration controllers deployed in over 700 major retail locations across France. These cyberattacks caused considerable material damage, fires, and food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.

The agency recognized that “this is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory.”

The incident highlights the potential consequences of cyberattacks against connected systems outside traditional IT networks, particularly refrigeration infrastructure used to preserve food supplies and maintain supermarket operations. Reported damage ranged from spoiled inventory and equipment failures, underscoring how attacks on OT (operational technology) infrastructure can translate into direct economic losses and disruption to services relied on by the public.

“In accordance with the 2026 national cybersecurity strategy, France is determined to use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace,” the agency added. “Consequently, France will summon the Ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran to France to express its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks.”

Furthermore, France will propose to its European partners the adoption of new sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved in this cyberattack against it, as well as in other malicious cyber activities.
Finally, France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.
In response, Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as ‘baseless and hostile.’
On Tuesday, France summoned the Iranian ambassador and said it would be seeking European-level sanctions in response.
The EU said it would seek to provide a “swift and united response” pending discussion with member states.

“As the EU, we have consistently called on all states to refrain from malicious behavior in the cyberspace, and we will continue to address such malicious behavior, making use of all the tools that we have, also under the EU cyber diplomacy toolbox, including sanctions,” spokesman Anouar El Anouni said.

paragraphs: WASHINGTON—The artificial-intelligence boom that had powered the U.S. stock market and economy for months was coming undone.

Jensen Huang, the longtime CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia, had been ousted following revelations of two affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Investors were hitting sell on the entire AI trade.
President Trump told associates there was only one solution: getting Huang, a friend and ally, his job back.

Over the weekend, Attorney General Todd Blanche presented an opening. The nation’s top law enforcement officer informed Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Saturday that Huang wasn’t the target or the subject of any Justice Department investigation, adding that the department had no evidence to suggest that he had broken laws or was a national security risk, according to U.S. officials.
President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia.

The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang, became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.

Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August.

By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear.

Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight.

Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18, the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported.
Trump on Monday denied being briefed. Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.

The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz. Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone, compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis.

A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence.

Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war.
"Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses.
Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance.

Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street. The two have met or appeared together at least 15 times since Trump returned to office, according to a CNBC review of public records and news reports. Huang in June told The Associated Press that Trump even "calls me in the middle of the night."
At Trump's Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration, several Silicon Valley titans occupied prime seats, but Huang wasn't there. The two men had never met.

That changed on Jan. 31, 2025, when Huang visited the White House, capping a bruising week for Nvidia: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek had wiped $593 billion off the company's market value in a single day, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.
Two days before the meeting, Trump's money managers bought between $1 million and $5 million in Nvidia stock.

For Huang, much of the relationship hinged on access to China. In April 2025, the administration effectively halted sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China, prompting a $4.5 billion charge, according to an SEC filing. Huang argued that withholding U.S. chips would only accelerate China's development of its own.

The administration eventually relented. After another meeting with Trump in July 2025, Huang announced from Beijing that Nvidia expected to resume H20 sales. A week after Trump confirmed an August 2025 deal calling for 15% of the revenue from the company's chip sales to China to go to the U.S. government, his accounts also bought between $5 million and $25 million in Nvidia stock, one of several large tech investments that day.

Huang was also becoming a fixture of Trump's international diplomacy, joining him in Saudi Arabia and the U.K. Nvidia, already a $1 million donor to Trump's inaugural fund, would pledge another $25 million to his planned White House ballroom on condition of anonymity, The Washington Post first reported.
But behind the scenes, intelligence officials first briefed Trump last fall on Huang's relationship with the woman suspected of spying for China, The New York Times reported.

Trump nevertheless continued to ease restrictions on Nvidia's business in China, announcing Dec. 8 that the company could sell its more powerful H200 chips. His accounts had sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock four days earlier and bought more the day after.

In the first eight months of 2026, Trump's accounts made another 38 Nvidia trades worth a combined $9.4 million to $28.3 million, according to CNBC's analysis. A disclosure released Oct. 8 — the day Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science — showed purchases of up to $1.6 million and sales of up to $1 million in August alone.
Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia's board weighed his future last week, urging him to fight to keep his job, the Times reported.

With Huang out and Nvidia's shares tumbling, Trump described him Thursday as a "tremendous talent" who was "going through hell" — in the same interview in which he boasted of the market's record highs.

Trump is already floating a comeback for Huang, telling reporters Monday that reinstating him "certainly isn't a bad idea." But Nvidia's board is not considering his return, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because they were discussing internal matters."

Levent Alpöge's claim arrived one day after Anthropic's IPO, but the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved
Mon 23 Nov 2026 · 00:04 EST · 3 min read
One day after Anthropic went public, one of its mathematicians announced that the company’s AI may have done something humans have failed to do since 1859.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge said he worked with Anthropic’s Claude model to produce a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis. That is a 167-year-old problem and one of the most famous open questions in mathematics. Independent checks are still underway, so for now this is a claim, not a coronation.
Alpöge is a Turkish-American mathematician at Anthropic. He described the effort as a collaboration with Claude rather than a solo human achievement or a fully autonomous machine result.
The work reportedly ran for about six weeks. It started in early October and wrapped on November 16, 2026, four days before the announcement.
The output is large. The proof was formalized in Lean, a proof assistant: software designed to check every logical step so that nothing rests on a mathematician’s say-so.
The Lean archive contains approximately 175,000 source files and totals 239 MB. It comes paired with a four-page note that presumably serves as the human-readable summary.
Reports suggest the total machine-generated text could exceed 250,000 pages.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. Each carries a $1 million award from the Clay Mathematics Institute.
As of now, the institute continues to list the hypothesis as unsolved. That is not a snub. It is how the process works.
To be eligible for the prize, a solution needs a peer-reviewed publication. It then faces a two-year scrutiny period. So even in the best case, the check is not getting cut anytime soon.
This is not the first time Alpöge has made noise in 2026. Earlier this year, he was credited with breakthroughs that included counterexamples to the Jacobian and Carathéodory conjectures.

A counterexample shows a conjecture is false by finding a case where it breaks. Proving a conjecture true across every case is a different and usually harder task. The Riemann claim falls in that second, more demanding category.
Anthropic priced its IPO on November 19, 2026, at $83 per share. The Riemann announcement landed the very next day.
The source material does not link the two events, and there is no indication the timing was coordinated. Still, the sequence is hard to ignore.

What to watch: the progress of independent verification of the Lean archive, whether a peer-reviewed paper appears, and whether the Clay Institute changes the problem’s status. The two-year scrutiny clock does not start until publication, so patience is mandatory.

For now, the most accurate summary is the boring one. A credible mathematician says Claude helped him prove one of math’s hardest problems. The machine checked its own homework, and the humans are now checking the machine.

paragraphs: The Nvidia soap opera took another wild turn Monday when its board announced Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. Investors loved it, and sent Nvidia’s shares up more than 30% while other AI stocks pared losses from last week’s rout. Call it the Donald Trump market put, but his extraordinary political intervention will have legal and political costs.

Mr. Trump proudly claimed credit for the board’s decision to bring Mr. Huang back less than two weeks after he was pushed out. “I convinced them,” he told CNBC. “I made the deal.” The board “did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” he added. “And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot.”
While analysts view Huang's return as largely positive for Nvidia and the broader AI trade, some say the AI chipmaker is not out of the woods yet.
Huang will appear before Congress committees for questioning on Dec. 1.
Retail sentiment for NVDA dipped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish.'

As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Congress hearing looms, President Donald Trump has said his government could potentially pardon him if he is indicted, while adding that he didn't think such an act would be necessary.

The President even said he has thought about having the U.S. government take a stake in Nvidia, similar to its stake in Intel in 2025, saying "it's probably not too late," according to comments made to the New York Post.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
Huang, one of the most prominent figures in the AI industry, was reinstated by Nvidia's board on Monday in a reversal after Trump intervened on his behalf.
Trump told the Post that it was his understanding that Huang had not had affairs with other women linked to Beijing and that he did not know how many affairs Huang had acknowledged.
NVDA stock rallied 31.5% the same day, but the rally lost steam. Shares dipped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session and another 2.2% in overnight trading.
While Huang's return as Nvidia chief is a major shot in the arm for the company and the broader AI trade, some commentators say the AI chipmaker is not out of the woods yet.

On Dec. 1, Huang will appear for a closed-door meeting with the House Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence committees on topics including his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, and his company's security protocols. He will testify before the Senate Banking Committee later that week.

Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang, saying Congress should tighten restrictions on China's access to the company's advanced AI chips and scrutinize the circumstances surrounding Huang's return, Reuters reported.
Still, some remain confident for Nvidia, given the record demand for AI servers and Huang's track record as an excellent leader and deal-maker.

"Even using a new formula discounting for affairs and every possible risk method and outcome. With Jensen at Nvidia. My Nvidia chips using AI analysis come up with $242 a share," Ross Gerber, CEO of investment firm Gerber Kawasaki, said in an X post, signaling a 56% upside.
Timothy Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, sold $4.5 million worth of company shares, according to an exchange filing on Tuesday. The divestiture was through several trades made on Nov. 19.
On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for NVDA dipped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish' as of late Tuesday, and message volume dipped to 'high' from 'extremely high.'
"$NVDA The most profitable AI company, with a CEO backed by the president of the US who needs him to succeed... and at a discount. What else do we need?" said a trader.
Another, with a contrarian view, wrote: "$NVDA Trump can only shield him for one more month .Come January Dems are gonna expose him as a traitor . This goes under $125 easy."
Year-to-date, NVDA stock is down 16.5%.

https://www.wsj.com/opinion/nvidia-jense.article_content:
The Nvidia soap opera took another wild turn Monday when its board announced Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. Investors loved it, and sent Nvidia’s shares up more than 30% while other AI stocks pared losses from last week’s rout. Call it the Donald Trump market put, but his extraordinary political intervention will have legal and political costs.

Mr. Trump proudly claimed credit for the board’s decision to bring Mr. Huang back less than two weeks after he was pushed out. “I convinced them,” he told CNBC. “I made the deal.” The board “did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” he added. “And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot.”

While analysts view Huang's return as largely positive for Nvidia and the broader AI trade, some say the AI chipmaker is not out of the woods yet.

Huang will appear before Congress committees for questioning on Dec. 1.

Retail sentiment for NVDA dipped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish.'

As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Congress hearing looms, President Donald Trump has said his government could potentially pardon him if he is indicted, while adding that he didn't think such an act would be necessary.

The President even said he has thought about having the U.S. government take a stake in Nvidia, similar to its stake in Intel in 2025, saying "it's probably not too late," according to comments made to the New York Post.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Huang, one of the most prominent figures in the AI industry, was reinstated by Nvidia's board on Monday in a reversal after Trump intervened on his behalf.

Trump told the Post that it was his understanding that Huang had not had affairs with other women linked to Beijing and that he did not know how many affairs Huang had acknowledged.

NVDA stock rallied 31.5% the same day, but the rally lost steam. Shares dipped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session and another 2.2% in overnight trading.

While Huang's return as Nvidia chief is a major shot in the arm for the company and the broader AI trade, some commentators say the AI chipmaker is not out of the woods yet.

On Dec. 1, Huang will appear for a closed-door meeting with the House Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence committees on topics including his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, and his company's security protocols. He will testify before the Senate Banking Committee later that week.

Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang, saying Congress should tighten restrictions on China's access to the company's advanced AI chips and scrutinize the circumstances surrounding Huang's return, Reuters reported.

Still, some remain confident for Nvidia, given the record demand for AI servers and Huang's track record as an excellent leader and deal-maker.

"Even using a new formula discounting for affairs and every possible risk method and outcome. With Jensen at Nvidia. My Nvidia chips using AI analysis come up with $242 a share," Ross Gerber, CEO of investment firm Gerber Kawasaki, said in an X post, signaling a 56% upside.

Timothy Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, sold $4.5 million worth of company shares, according to an exchange filing on Tuesday. The divestiture was through several trades made on Nov. 19.

On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for NVDA dipped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish' as of late Tuesday, and message volume dipped to 'high' from 'extremely high.'

"$NVDA The most profitable AI company, with a CEO backed by the president of the US who needs him to succeed... and at a discount. What else do we need?" said a trader.

Another, with a contrarian view, wrote: "$NVDA Trump can only shield him for one more month .Come January Dems are gonna expose him as a traitor . This goes under $125 easy."

Year-to-date, NVDA stock is down 16.5%.

Silicon Valley divorce lawyers are seeing a surge in outreach from CEOs, founders, and high-net-worth employees who are citing the Nvidia scandal as the reason for their calls, according to Fortune’s Emily Forlini.
The revelation of Jensen Huang’s affairs is a “precautionary tale for other CEOs,” said one lawyer who has been involved in the high-profile divorces of some of the tech industry’s most famous CEOs.

Jensen and Lori Huang have been married for 41 years, and reportedly do not have a prenuptial agreement. Jensen Huang is one of the richest people in the world, with a net worth of roughly $137 billion. If Lori leaves, a huge chunk of Jensen’s net worth would potentially transfer to her.

In addition to pursuing prenuptial agreements, many are interested in drafting nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) for their significant others, which is a new trend, says Monica Mazzei, a partner in Buchalter’s San Francisco family law office.

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh will almost certainly add another 0.5% to U.S. interest rates in December, according to the CME FedWatch futures index, and Wall Street is angsty that the move will cause a recession. “The Fed will put the U.S. and [the] world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%,” Bill Ackman said recently.
“The economy is super strong right now, but the Fed is about to kill it,” Jamie Cox of the Harris Financial Group ($1.5 billion AUM) told Fortune.

The problem is that inflation—which at 3.7% is high above the Fed’s 2% target—is being driven by the price of oil (which the Fed can do nothing about) and the price of computer chips and tech equipment (which the Fed can also do nothing about).

If the Fed increases interest rates, it may derail areas of the economy that are sensitive to higher borrowing costs while doing nothing about the roaring trade in oil. AI is increasingly dependent on debt funding, and higher rates could kill off that liquidity.

“Tech drove 44% of GDP growth [in the last 12 months], leaving growth vulnerable as capex slows,” according to Wells Fargo’s Ohsung Kwon. “The fear is hikes into a slowdown, and an overly hawkish Fed could potentially drive recession fears.”

Obviously, the situation with Iran is out of the Fed’s control. But as Fortune’s Ellie Pringle noted yesterday, if Warsh continues to “look through” oil-driven inflation then bond investors will start questioning the Fed’s credibility.
“The path of the war is crucial for the Fed's path,” Kwon said in a note.

Investors have continued to dump tech stocks over the past 24 hours on continued worries about the stability of the AI trade and a report that the Trump administration was proposing a new set of trade tariffs on China, Europe, and 14 other countries. S&P 500 futures moved lower ahead of the open in New York.
“The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours,” Jim Reid and his team at Deutsche Bank said this morning.

At UBS, Paul Donovan said: “The concern is the impact on U.S. inflation, and thus U.S. interest rates. Reports suggest U.S. importers will face only modest tariffs on goods from several countries. There is less certainty about goods from China, but U.S. importers became adept at avoiding those tariffs. A 10% tariff on a finished good translates into around a 4% consumer price increase, as tariffs occur early in supply chains.”

The tech sector saw the worst losses. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 1.48% yesterday, much farther than the broader market. In fact, the equal-weight S&P 500—a notional index that values each stock equally—rose 0.53%, suggesting buyers in a range of non-tech stocks.
S&P 500 futures were down again this morning, but Nasdaq 100 futures slipped even farther: down 2.39%, another big step down for an index of its size.

The S&P 500 may have flirted with a downward “correction” around the Nvidia drama, but it’s nowhere near an official bear market, defined by a decline of 20% from the peak. In fact, a bear market is unlikely to happen, according to Deutsche Bank’s Henry Allen. The bank’s official forecast is for the S&P 500 to hit a heady 9,000 by the end of next year.

“It’s worth bearing in mind that the outright bear markets of the last 50 years (S&P 500 down 20% or more) have previously occurred when there was at least one of (1) a recession, (2) widespread expectations of a recession, or (3) after a Fed tightening cycle with multiple hikes.”
Note to self: We will officially be in a tightening cycle if the Fed raises interest rates in December, which it is widely expected to do.

“Since Q4 2021, nonresidential construction employment has outgrown residential by 13.2% in the typical state among the 10 with the highest data center spending, versus 3.5% elsewhere,” according to Matthew Martin of Oxford Economics.
“If these 10 states had followed the rest of the country, up to 45,000 more workers would be in residential construction – about 24,000 of them in specialty trades,” he noted.

The price at which lifting an AI data center into orbit will fall below the cost of building one on Earth, if Elon Musk’s SpaceX can achieve routine and rapid rocket reuse, according to an estimate by ARK Invest’s Tasha Keeney. The price is currently $1,000 per kilo.

Fanatics has become a one-stop shop for sports fans looking to rep their favorite teams and athletes, and now generates roughly $14 billion in annual revenue. For cofounder and CEO Michael Rubin, however, the road to building that empire nearly ended before he turned 20.

When Rubin was just 13, he started a business selling ski equipment out of his parents’ basement in Pennsylvania. A year later, he opened his own storefront. He was making money quickly—and even bought a Porsche before he could legally drive.

But around 1988, there was an unusually warm winter, and so his customers weren’t coming. “It didn’t snow that year,” Rubin recalled recently. “End of the year, I had $200,000 of bills, $80,000 of inventory, and I was sitting right in front of bankruptcy.”

To dig himself out, he negotiated his debts down to $35,000, borrowed money from neighbors, and used the proceeds from a new venture in the closeout business to repay his loans. Five years later, at 21, Rubin was generating $150 million in sales buying and selling closeout merchandise.

“I went from death in its eyes, bankrupt, thought I was a complete failure, giving up on entrepreneurship, to five years later, doing $150 million, making $10 to $15 million a year as a kid,” Rubin said. “And so to me, each disaster, if you learn from it, leads to your next success.”

When Rubin was just 13, he started a business selling ski equipment out of his parents’ basement in Pennsylvania. A year later, he opened his own storefront. He was making money quickly—and even bought a Porsche before he could legally drive.

But around 1988, there was an unusually warm winter, and so his customers weren’t coming. “It didn’t snow that year,” Rubin recalled recently. “End of the year, I had $200,000 of bills, $80,000 of inventory, and I was sitting right in front of bankruptcy.”

paragraphs: Leopold Aschenbrenner, whose Situational Awareness hedge fund nearly unraveled over the summer after its borrowing-fueled bets on artificial intelligence soured, told investors it lost 65% after fees in the third quarter as it worked to learn from its mistakes.

The fund is up 88.5% after fees for the year through September, Aschenbrenner said in an investor letter seen by The Wall Street Journal, telling clients that investing opportunities today “are the highest potential return we have seen in the lifetime of the fund.”

(Bloomberg) -- Situational Awareness told investors it lost 65% after fees in the third quarter, after highly levered bets on artificial intelligence firms nearly led to the hedge fund’s implosion in July, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The hedge fund is still up 88.5% after fees for the year through the month of September, founder Leopold Aschenbrenner said in a letter viewed by the Wall Street Journal. Despite the tumult, the fund stills sees opportunities to invest with high potential for return, according to the report.

Situational Awareness was pushed to the brink in July as a brief moment of panic about AI spread across global markets, sparking margin calls from banks and turning it into a symbol of the wild swings that have accompanied the AI trade. The firm ultimately sold a large chunk of its public equities portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel.

Aschenbrenner, who named his firm after a viral essay he wrote in 2024, has focused on firms he thinks will benefit from the AI revolution. He quickly became known for using leverage to ramp up his returns and his risks.

Aschenbrenner said in the letter that he was taking a more measured approach to risk management, having learned a lesson from the recent turmoil. “Volatility, yes; existential risk, even if we are totally wrong, never,” he reportedly told investors.

The third quarter performance referenced in the letter does not capture the more recent selloff in the market during the month of October, when valuations of AI companies came under scrutiny and wild swings in stocks tied to the artificial intelligence buildout have made it an even more complicated market for investors to navigate.

Aschenbrenner wrote in the letter that Situational Awareness’s portfolio was composed of about 70% publicly traded stocks and 30% positions in private companies following the IPO of Anthropic, its largest private position, according to the report. The firm may rebalance its portfolio away from Anthropic, though it’s “highly bullish” at the IPO price, the WSJ reported.

paragraphs: Tech experts are warning that a global memory chip shortage driven by technology giants is causing prices to soar for many consumer electronic products.
“All these AI data centres that are powering all these AI tools, they need huge amounts of RAM and they are basically gobbling it up right now,” said Mike Agerbo from GetConnected Media.

Memory chips or RAM (Random Access Memory) are in short supply around the world. RAM allows your computer to access data quickly and efficiently; however, major tech companies, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta are buying up the global supply to fuel their AI centres.

That’s leaving less RAM for the traditional electronics market. Given the shortage, industry experts predict prices for many consumer electronic products like laptops, tablets, and even smartphones will increase by as much as 20 per cent or higher.
“I think we’re going to be looking at rapid price increases over the next 12 to 24 months minimum,” Dwight Dubowits of North Vancouver’s Concept Computers told Consumer Matters.
Dubowits has been in the computer business for over 40 years and says the shortage of RAM is causing a seismic shift in the industry.
“I think the $600 laptop and cheap desktop market has pretty much disappeared at this point,” he said.
“Entry level is in the $800-$900 range. We see that going as high as $1,200 or $1,300 just to get a basic function, reasonable quality laptop computer.”

Dubowits also says some local dealers are being forced to reduce costs by offering systems with less RAM. “Consumers should ensure that these systems are, in fact, upgradable,” said Dubowits. “Many systems, especially laptops, have limited or no capacity for adding more RAM post-purchase.”
The shortage is also hitting the gaming industry especially hard. GamerTech Toronto builds custom gaming desktop computers and says it’s spending four times as much for RAM on its computers.

“Basically, the entire cost to build the computer has increased and so we are having to pass that along for the actual sale price,” said Niam Radia from GamerTech Toronto. “This may just be the new normal for RAM pricing and PC part pricing overall.”
Three major companies manufacture and control most of the world’s memory chips and experts predict this shortage could continue well into 2027.

“I would recommend looking at purchasing a computing device now. If you’ve been thinking about it in the next six months, I’d get it now because I can only see the prices basically going up,” Agerbo said.

“Basically, the entire cost to build the computer has increased and so we are having to pass that along for the actual sale price,” said Niam Radia from GamerTech Toronto. “This may just be the new normal for RAM pricing and PC part pricing overall.”

Three major companies manufacture and control most of the world’s memory chips and experts predict this shortage could continue well into 2027.

“I would recommend looking at purchasing a computing device now. If you’ve been thinking about it in the next six months, I’d get it now because I can only see the prices basically going up,” Agerbo said.

paragraphs: From a difficult childhood to the heights of Silicon Valley, Jensen Huang built an AI empire. But a widening scandal has brought his reign to an end.
In 2024, when asked what advice he would have for aspiring Stanford entrepreneurs, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang repeated one of his signature lines.
“I wish upon you ample doses of pain and suffering,” he said onstage at a summit (opens in new tab) for the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research.
Greatness, he said, comes from character. And character is formed through suffering. “Unfortunately, resilience matters in success,” he said.

Huang, 63, has endured a very public test of his own character — one that has brought his extraordinary 33-year reign at Nvidia to an abrupt end, at the height of the company’s success. On Sunday, he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, and on Wednesday, The New York Times (opens in new tab) reported he’d been in another extramarital relationship, this time with a healthcare executive at his own company who reports to him. By Thursday morning, Huang had resigned.

Nvidia has named longtime CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor. Kress will continue serving as CFO. The company has also appointed longtime director Harvey C. Jones as its first board chair, a significant change in governance for a business dominated by Huang since its founding.

Huang’s remarkable fall captures a pivotal moment in Silicon Valley. Money and economic influence are being consolidated among a handful of hundred-billion- and trillion-dollar AI companies, all racing to build a potentially society-altering technology ahead of rivals in China and other countries. The heads of the biggest AI players have become public figures, their brands melding with the companies they run.

For Nvidia, the scandal presents unique challenges, beyond a CEO’s infidelity. The woman who is suspected of sending information to China was an executive at a Singapore-based company that bought billions of dollars worth of equipment from Nvidia – some of which may have reached China. Huang was deeply involved in running Nvidia, with 60 direct reports. He said he worked seven days a week and was reported to have an Nvidia tattoo. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Huang didn’t believe in succession planning, raising questions about how the company will manage the sudden departure of the man who led it for decades.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to Thailand, and when he was 9, his parents sent him and his brother to live with relatives in Washington state to escape social unrest. His aunt and uncle sent the siblings to a Kentucky facility that turned out to be more reform school than prep school. Huang said he scrubbed all the toilets in the dorm building every day, learned to play table tennis, and taught his much older roommate how to read.
“I remember that part of my life more vividly than just about any other,” he told Wired in 2002.

Soon, Huang’s parents joined the boys in the U.S., and the family settled down in Oregon. His teenage years were filled with part-time jobs — busboy, dishwasher, and waiter at Denny’s — while he excelled at school and table tennis. He became a nationally ranked player and graduated from high school early to study electrical engineering at Oregon State.

It was there, when he was 17, that he met Lori Mills, who was also studying electrical engineering. His pickup line, according to “The Nvidia Way,” a biography by Tae Kim, was “Do you want to see my homework?”

After graduation, the couple married and moved to San Jose so Huang could take a job designing microchips at AMD, kicking off his decades-long career in semiconductors. He attended Stanford part time while holding down his day job, slowly earning a master’s degree in electrical engineering. He moved on to another Silicon Valley chipmaker, LSI Logic, where he worked with Sun Microsystems.

Starting in 1992, Huang and two Sun employees, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, sketched out the vision for Nvidia during regular visits to a Denny’s in San Jose. According to The Wall Street Journal, the trio set up shop there for so long that the staff eventually moved them to a back room.

Nvidia was officially founded in 1993 — the NV in the name stood for “next version,” according to Fortune — and its first office was set up in Sunnyvale, located by an expressway and a Wells Fargo branch. Its vision was to make better 3D graphics chips for gaming PCs. The company’s first product, the NV1, failed; its second was canceled; and the third, the Riva 128, featured an entirely different design.

“We built Riva 128 just as we were running out of money. The Riva 128 shocked the young 3D market, put us on the map, and saved the company,” Huang said in a 2023 commencement (opens in new tab) speech at National Taiwan University.

Until recently, coverage of the family’s life had laid out a neat, unremarkable narrative. Huang mentions his marriage, and his wife’s support, frequently in interviews. “I have a perfect life,” he said at the Stanford event. Asked about his famous black leather jacket, Huang said his wife picked it out.
“This is what my wife bought for me, and this is what I’m wearing,” he said. “I do zero percent of my own shopping.”

The couple had two children in quick succession while Huang was moving up in his career. Now in their 30s, both the kids have high-profile jobs at Nvidia. After studying baking and working in the food industry, his daughter Madison Huang worked at LVMH and earned an MBA at London Business School. She started as an intern at Nvidia in 2020 and is now senior director of product marketing for physical AI. Spencer Huang started as an intern in 2010, according to his LinkedIn, then opened a cocktail bar in Taipei. He has been back at Nvidia for more than four years and is the director of robotics product.

Huang has addressed concerns about nepotism, according to The Information, saying parents would only recommend hiring children who wouldn’t embarrass them. The report also said Malachowsky and board member Aarti Shah have children who work at the company.

In 2017, Huang planted roots in San Francisco. He is reported to have purchased a Pacific Heights mansion for $38 million. Through their foundation, Huang and his wife have pledged a $75 million matching gift to create the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design in San Francisco. They’ve also committed $5 million a year to the San Francisco Opera.

In 1999, Nvidia went public, its shares priced at $12 apiece. The plan was always for Huang to run the business side of Nvidia, while Malachowsky managed hardware and Priem software. Priem left in 2003, and Malachowsky kept a low profile, leaving Huang as the public face of the company.

Like Steve Jobs before him, Huang took the classic Silicon Valley route of adopting a signature look. His was the black leather jacket, which gave him a slightly cooler, midlife-crisis air than most tech CEOs. In the 2000s, his public persona grew with long profiles, professional photo shoots, keynote speeches, and conference appearances. In 2017, Fortune named him Businessperson of the Year. Still, the dry nature of the chip business kept him from being as much of a household name as the heads of consumer-facing companies, including Apple’s Jobs, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Google’s founders.

He’d had a history of talking about potential markets of the future — what he called “zero billion markets.” AI was one of those bets that paid off spectacularly. Huang said in the National Taiwan University commencement speech that once Nvidia saw deep learning’s potential, it turned all its resources to the technology. In 2007, the company released software called CUDA that made it possible for its chips to be used for more than just graphics. Nividia built it into every gaming card, despite the cost — a bet that paid off when early AI researchers discovered the technology. The company focused on selling to data centers and designing the chips that would eventually power the AI boom.

In 2016, Huang personally delivered Nvidia’s DGX-1 AI supercomputer to Elon Musk at OpenAI, which at the time was a nonprofit research lab. Nvidia increased its business with big tech companies, cloud companies, AI labs, and governments.

In May 2023, after a particularly positive earnings forecast, the company’s market value rose by $184 billion in one day. Huang’s own net worth shot up $6 billion. On May 30, Nvidia reached a $1 trillion market capitalization, and a year later it briefly became the most valuable public company in the world. Now, the vast majority of chips used to power AI are designed by Nvidia.
It was during this rapid rise that reports first linked Huang to Alice Huang, with whom he has admitted to having an affair.

His power showed up in unexpected places. Oracle CTO Larry Ellison joked on an earnings call that he and Musk were “begging Jensen for GPUs” at a dinner at Nobu Palo Alto. Huang became close to President Donald Trump, lobbying him to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China.

Since Trump’s return to office, Huang has been at the forefront of a growing alliance between Silicon Valley’s AI’s titans and the administration. He has become a frequent visitor to the White House, pushing back against tighter AI regulation. His influence even extended to policymaking: Trump appointed him to a presidential science and technology advisory council and awarded him the National Medal of Science in 2026.

Huang spent 33 years making Nvidia indispensable to the technology industry. In the process, he may also have made himself indispensable to Nvidia. Now following his abrupt departure at the height of the AI boom, the company faces a question: What happens without him?

Nvidia has named longtime CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor. Kress will continue serving as CFO. The company has also appointed longtime director Harvey C. Jones as its first board chair, a significant change in governance for a business dominated by Huang since its founding.

Huang’s remarkable fall captures a pivotal moment in Silicon Valley. Money and economic influence are being consolidated among a handful of hundred-billion- and trillion-dollar AI companies, all racing to build a potentially society-altering technology ahead of rivals in China and other countries. The heads of the biggest AI players have become public figures, their brands melding with the companies they run.

For Nvidia, the scandal presents unique challenges, beyond a CEO’s infidelity. The woman who is suspected of sending information to China was an executive at a Singapore-based company that bought billions of dollars worth of equipment from Nvidia – some of which may have reached China. Huang was deeply involved in running Nvidia, with 60 direct reports. He said he worked seven days a week and was reported to have an Nvidia tattoo. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Huang didn’t believe in succession planning, raising questions about how the company will manage the sudden departure of the man who led it for decades.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to Thailand, and when he was 9, his parents sent him and his brother to live with relatives in Washington state to escape social unrest. His aunt and uncle sent the siblings to a Kentucky facility that turned out to be more reform school than prep school. Huang said he scrubbed all the toilets in the dorm building every day, learned to play table tennis, and taught his much older roommate how to read.

“I remember that part of my life more vividly than just about any other,” he told Wired in 2002.

Soon, Huang’s parents joined the boys in the U.S., and the family settled down in Oregon. His teenage years were filled with part-time jobs — busboy, dishwasher, and waiter at Denny’s — while he excelled at school and table tennis. He became a nationally ranked player and graduated from high school early to study electrical engineering at Oregon State.

It was there, when he was 17, that he met Lori Mills, who was also studying electrical engineering. His pickup line, according to “The Nvidia Way,” a biography by Tae Kim, was “Do you want to see my homework?”

After graduation, the couple married and moved to San Jose so Huang could take a job designing microchips at AMD, kicking off his decades-long career in semiconductors. He attended Stanford part time while holding down his day job, slowly earning a master’s degree in electrical engineering. He moved on to another Silicon Valley chipmaker, LSI Logic, where he worked with Sun Microsystems.

Starting in 1992, Huang and two Sun employees, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, sketched out the vision for Nvidia during regular visits to a Denny’s in San Jose. According to The Wall Street Journal, the trio set up shop there for so long that the staff eventually moved them to a back room.

Nvidia was officially founded in 1993 — the NV in the name stood for “next version,” according to Fortune — and its first office was set up in Sunnyvale, located by an expressway and a Wells Fargo branch. Its vision was to make better 3D graphics chips for gaming PCs. The company’s first product, the NV1, failed; its second was canceled; and the third, the Riva 128, featured an entirely different design.

“We built Riva 128 just as we were running out of money. The Riva 128 shocked the young 3D market, put us on the map, and saved the company,” Huang said in a 2023 commencement (opens in new tab) speech at National Taiwan University.

Until recently, coverage of the family’s life had laid out a neat, unremarkable narrative. Huang mentions his marriage, and his wife’s support, frequently in interviews. “I have a perfect life,” he said at the Stanford event. Asked about his famous black leather jacket, Huang said his wife picked it out.

“This is what my wife bought for me, and this is what I’m wearing,” he said. “I do zero percent of my own shopping.”

The couple had two children in quick succession while Huang was moving up in his career. Now in their 30s, both the kids have high-profile jobs at Nvidia. After studying baking and working in the food industry, his daughter Madison Huang worked at LVMH and earned an MBA at London Business School. She started as an intern at Nvidia in 2020 and is now senior director of product marketing for physical AI. Spencer Huang started as an intern in 2010, according to his LinkedIn, then opened a cocktail bar in Taipei. He has been back at Nvidia for more than four years and is the director of robotics product.

Huang has addressed concerns about nepotism, according to The Information, saying parents would only recommend hiring children who wouldn’t embarrass them. The report also said Malachowsky and board member Aarti Shah have children who work at the company.

In 2017, Huang planted roots in San Francisco. He is reported to have purchased a Pacific Heights mansion for $38 million. Through their foundation, Huang and his wife have pledged a $75 million matching gift to create the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design in San Francisco. They’ve also committed $5 million a year to the San Francisco Opera.

In 1999, Nvidia went public, its shares priced at $12 apiece. The plan was always for Huang to run the business side of Nvidia, while Malachowsky managed hardware and Priem software. Priem left in 2003, and Malachowsky kept a low profile, leaving Huang as the public face of the company.

Like Steve Jobs before him, Huang took the classic Silicon Valley route of adopting a signature look. His was the black leather jacket, which gave him a slightly cooler, midlife-crisis air than most tech CEOs. In the 2000s, his public persona grew with long profiles, professional photo shoots, keynote speeches, and conference appearances. In 2017, Fortune named him Businessperson of the Year. Still, the dry nature of the chip business kept him from being as much of a household name as the heads of consumer-facing companies, including Apple’s Jobs, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Google’s founders.

He’d had a history of talking about potential markets of the future — what he called “zero billion markets.” AI was one of those bets that paid off spectacularly. Huang said in the National Taiwan University commencement speech that once Nvidia saw deep learning’s potential, it turned all its resources to the technology. In 2007, the company released software called CUDA that made it possible for its chips to be used for more than just graphics. Nividia built it into every gaming card, despite the cost — a bet that paid off when early AI researchers discovered the technology. The company focused on selling to data centers and designing the chips that would eventually power the AI boom.

In 2016, Huang personally delivered Nvidia’s DGX-1 AI supercomputer to Elon Musk at OpenAI, which at the time was a nonprofit research lab. Nvidia increased its business with big tech companies, cloud companies, AI labs, and governments.

In May 2023, after a particularly positive earnings forecast, the company’s market value rose by $184 billion in one day. Huang’s own net worth shot up $6 billion. On May 30, Nvidia reached a $1 trillion market capitalization, and a year later it briefly became the most valuable public company in the world. Now, the vast majority of chips used to power AI are designed by Nvidia.

It was during this rapid rise that reports first linked Huang to Alice Huang, with whom he has admitted to having an affair.

His power showed up in unexpected places. Oracle CTO Larry Ellison joked on an earnings call that he and Musk were “begging Jensen for GPUs” at a dinner at Nobu Palo Alto. Huang became close to President Donald Trump, lobbying him to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China.

Since Trump’s return to office, Huang has been at the forefront of a growing alliance between Silicon Valley’s AI’s titans and the administration. He has become a frequent visitor to the White House, pushing back against tighter AI regulation. His influence even extended to policymaking: Trump appointed him to a presidential science and technology advisory council and awarded him the National Medal of Science in 2026.

Huang spent 33 years making Nvidia indispensable to the technology industry. In the process, he may also have made himself indispensable to Nvidia. Now following his abrupt departure at the height of the AI boom, the company faces a question: What happens without him?
